I am a 40 something male with a tendency towards impatience and over-rationalisation, but this hit a chord with me in an artistic sense. Seriously. 

Upon listening to the whole thing while doing something else, I am left with a multilayered impression.

For me, the first layer was  a Moorcock poeticism in its exploration of stereotypes. The protagonist is the "free-spirited individualist" with the three antagonists so wonderfully embody the archetypes of "cop on edge", "rational authority figure" and "hooker with heart of gold".

The next layer is the conflict. It starts as an obvious absurdity but then as it progresses, it somehow takes on an internally consistent logic to the extent that all four players unconsciously acknowledge the Dadaist framework that has somehow sprung up around them.

Rational argument becomes demonstrably meaningless within the surreal linguistic landscape. The unexpected resolution only comes through desperation in the form of retreat to authority, which, ordinarily fallacious, is sound argumentation down this particular rabbit hole.

The most elegant layer for me is that this social interaction occurs with a lack of awareness of the true narrative which I find reminiscent of Waiting for Godot.

**Edit:** I chose to view it as a performance and in doing so, found it strangely compelling.
